subject: Nariway Daily Check-in - 2026-08-19
html:
Nariway Daily Check-in

19 August 2026

Needs your attention / action today

  • Confirm or pull the Table 1 wealth-manager figure before the report ships. This week's QA audit caught the flagship report citing "~51% of wealth managers now offer art services, up from ~25% in 2011" as a settled fact — but the claims register's own entry for that number says to confirm the exact figure before citing publicly, and separately flags the trend direction may be backwards. Check it against the actual Deloitte Art & Finance report, or pull/caveat the row until you do.
  • Send the Ruth Fine email. Still unsent since it was drafted last Saturday — zero cost, ready to go, and the concrete next step your own editorial-direction doc names for the Vogel conversation.

Today I learned

Even a binding "agreed value" art insurance policy doesn't end a valuation dispute. Billionaire collector Ronald Perelman sued a five-carrier syndicate (Lloyd's underwriters, AIG, Great Lakes, Swiss Re, Chubb) for $410 million after a 2018 fire at his estate, arguing "invisible damage" had cost five Warhol, Ruscha, and Twombly works their "spark" even though nothing was visibly damaged. A New York judge rejected the claim in September 2025. It's the insurance-side mirror of a finding already in the report on the tax side (the IRS Art Advisory Panel adjusts about 65% of audited appraisals): even sophisticated parties with a binding contract still can't agree what art is worth. Source note: market-intelligence #9.

What changed, and what it means

  • The case dataset grew for the first time in three days, and its target changed. Four new corporate/international cases (UBS Art Collection, Fondazione Prada, Muzej Lah — the sample's first Central European museum, and the Reader's Digest/Wallace Collection) brought the coded count to 54, plus a fifth case, Casabianca (De Santis family, Lake Como), filed separately via Signals. This follows your decision this week to lift the original 50-case cap, so the target is now ~75 cases near-term and ~100 eventually, growing alongside depth work rather than switching to depth-only.
  • The report's insurance chapter got its first real sourcing. The headline finding is a data-quality one: published fine-art-insurance market-size figures disagree by roughly 100x across vendors, so the report deliberately does not cite a number, only the underwriting structure (Lloyd's Fine Art & Specie syndicates) and the Perelman case above.
  • QA caught a new critical. The report's own Table 1 currently states an unconfirmed figure as fact (see action item above) — the second-straight-week open finding on live Substack copy is a known, deliberately deferred, low-priority item and needs nothing from you right now.
  • A hygiene sweep fixed four broken internal links and two cases' drifted frontmatter — routine upkeep, nothing for you to do.

Where we stand

Still $0 earned, and H7B (will anyone pay) is exactly as untested as it was a week ago. The report keeps compounding as a scalable asset toward the million-dollar goal — now growing in both breadth and depth rather than holding at a fixed count — but the two cheapest, zero-cost moves that would touch the revenue question directly, sending the Ruth Fine email and fact-checking one report figure, are both still undone.

Brief for the board: marketing/events/events-radar.md still describes the Opal Family Office Legacy Summit as "Reopened… pending Dawn confirming the room," and yesterday's CMO brief repeated that framing. The actual decision record (company/decisions/2026-08-12-opal-summit.md) shows it was briefly reopened and then declined final on 2026-08-13. Worth a quick correction in events-radar so it stops reading as an open question six days before the event passes.
